# Introduction

High-content imaging measures the morphology of single cells in detail.
In a Cell Painting experiment, cells are stained with dyes for several
organelles, imaged, and segmented, and CellProfiler measures about 1,000
features of every cell: its size and shape, the intensity and texture of
each stain, how the stains are distributed between the nucleus and the cell
edge, and how two stains colocalize. Comparing these features between a
perturbation, such as a drug, and a control shows whether and how the
perturbation changes the cells.

cellpaintr is built for experiments with few biological replicates, such as
patient-derived cells from a handful of donors. The cells are abundant, but
the replicates are not, and the replicates, not the cells, are the
independent units. cellpaintr therefore learns on cells and tests on
replicates:

1. For each replicate, a random forest trained on the cells of all other
    replicates scores the cells of the held-out replicate with the
    probability of the perturbed condition (pre-validation with replicates
    as folds). Every score comes from a model that never saw that replicate.
2. A patient-level test compares the scores of the perturbed and the
    control cells of each replicate. Because the models of different
    held-out replicates are trained on each other's cells, their scores are
    correlated, and an ordinary paired t-test is too liberal. cellpaintr
    offers an exact permutation test and two corrected t-tests.
3. The test is repeated for interpretable feature groups, such as
    CellProfiler measurement types (intensity, texture, ...) or imaging
    channels, and summarized in a volcano plot.

Profiling pipelines such as pycytominer aggregate single cells into
well-level profiles and compare profiles by their similarity. cellpaintr
instead trains on single cells, so it learns the direction of an effect from
the data, which makes it powerful when all cells shift, even slightly, in
many features, and it detects changes in the spread or shape of a feature
distribution that leave the means unchanged. A strong response of a small
subpopulation of cells, on the other hand, is diluted in the mean score of a
replicate; a location test on replicate means, the standard patient-level
analysis, detects such responses more readily. It keeps the
data in a `SingleCellExperiment`, so that tools from Bioconductor
single-cell workflows, such as `scater` and `scrapper`, apply without
conversion.

# Installation

```{r install-package, eval=FALSE}
if (!require("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("cellpaintr")
```

```{r load-libs, message=FALSE}
library(cellpaintr)
library(scater)
library(scrapper)
library(purrr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggrepel)
```

# Input data

## What cellpaintr reads

cellpaintr reads the per-object table that CellProfiler's
ExportToSpreadsheet module writes for the cells, usually called
`MyExpt_Cells.csv`, with one row per cell. `loadData()` expects

- the column `ImageNumber`, which identifies the image (site) of each cell,
    and usually `ObjectNumber`;
- image metadata columns whose names start with `Metadata_`, such as
    `Metadata_Plate`, `Metadata_Well`, `Metadata_Patient`, and
    `Metadata_Drug`. CellProfiler adds them to the cell table with the option
    "Add image metadata columns to your object data file" of
    ExportToSpreadsheet; the plate layout (which drug and which patient are in
    which well) usually comes from a metadata file loaded with the Metadata
    module;
- numeric measurement columns, such as `AreaShape_Area`,
    `Intensity_MeanIntensity_DNA`, or `Texture_Contrast_Mito_3_00_256`. Their
    names follow CellProfiler's convention
    `<MeasurementType>_<Feature>_<Channel>_<Parameters>`, which cellpaintr
    uses to form feature groups.

`loadData()` turns the `Metadata_` columns, without the prefix, together
with `ImageNumber`, `ObjectNumber`, and the cell centre coordinates
`Location_Center_X`, `_Y`, and `_Z`, into the column data of the cells, and
all other columns into the assay `features`. If the metadata were exported
only to the image table (`MyExpt_Image.csv`), join them to the cells by
`ImageNumber` first:

```{r join-metadata, eval=FALSE}
cells <- readr::read_csv("MyExpt_Cells.csv")
images <- readr::read_csv("MyExpt_Image.csv") |>
    select(ImageNumber, starts_with("Metadata_"))
readr::write_csv(left_join(cells, images, by = "ImageNumber"), "cells.csv")
sce <- loadData("cells.csv")
```

## Example data from the JUMP Cell Painting Consortium

The package ships a small subset of the JUMP Cell Painting dataset
(cpg0016), released under CC0 by the JUMP Cell Painting Consortium through
the Cell Painting Gallery. U2OS cells were stained for DNA (Hoechst), RNA
(SYTO 14), actin, Golgi, and plasma membrane (AGP), and mitochondria (Mito),
and imaged with brightfield as well. The subset holds 240 cells from four
compound plates of one batch: the negative control DMSO and two of the
eight JUMP positive controls, AMG900, an Aurora kinase inhibitor with a
strong effect on morphology, and dexamethasone, a glucocorticoid with a weak
one. For each plate and compound, two random wells and, from each well, 10
random cells of one random site were kept, with all CellProfiler
measurements of the cell compartment. The script
`system.file("scripts", "make-jump-subset.R", package = "cellpaintr")`
documents how the subset was made.

These data have no patients. Plates take their place as the replicates:
every plate carries all three compounds, so the design is paired, as in a
drug screen on patient-derived cells where every patient's cells are imaged
with and without each drug.

```{r read-data}
cell_file <- system.file("extdata", "jump_subset.csv.gz",
    package = "cellpaintr"
)
sce <- loadData(cell_file)
sce
table(sce$Compound, sce$Plate)
```

# Preprocessing

## Cells and features

CellProfiler also exports columns that describe the segmentation rather than
the cells, such as the number of child objects or the object numbers of the
nearest neighbours. Remove them before modeling.

```{r remove-bookkeeping}
bookkeeping <- grepl(
    "^(Parent|Children)_|ObjectNumber",
    rownames(sce)
)
sce <- sce[!bookkeeping, ]
```

Remove cells with missing measurements, features without spread, and
features that are mostly zero, which often come from empty stains or
failed measurements.

```{r data-cleaning}
sce <- removeNAs(sce)
sce <- removeLowVariance(sce, robust = TRUE)
sce <- removeZeroInflation(sce, proportion = 0.2)
dim(sce)
```

In a full experiment, images with very few cells (out of focus, empty
wells) or very many cells (debris, clumps) are often of poor quality.
`plotCellsPerImage()` shows the number of cells per image, and
`removeOutliers()` removes the cells of images outside a range. The example
data keep only 10 cells of one site per well, so this step does not apply
here. Cell-level outliers can be removed with `scater`, for example cells
whose summed features lie more than three median absolute deviations from
the median.

```{r cells-per-image, eval=FALSE}
plotCellsPerImage(sce)
sce <- removeOutliers(sce, min = 20, max = 300)
qc <- perCellQCMetrics(sce, assay.type = "features")
sce <- sce[, !isOutlier(qc$sum)]
```

## Transformation and scaling

CellProfiler features live on different scales: intensities are positive
and skewed, correlations are bounded by -1 and 1, and some texture measures
are proportions. `transformScale()` transforms each family to an
approximately unbounded, symmetric scale (logarithm, Fisher's z, logit, or a
rank-based inverse normal transformation), caps infinite values at the
finite extremes of each feature, and standardizes every feature, here with
robust z-scores based on the median and the median absolute deviation. The
result is stored in the new assay `tfmfeatures`.

```{r transform-data}
sce <- transformScale(sce, robust = TRUE)
assayNames(sce)
```

## Plate effects

Plates often show gradients across rows and columns, for example from
evaporation at the edges. `removeRowColEffect()` fits Tukey's median polish
to the median of each feature in each well and subtracts the row and column
effects from every cell. It needs the factors `Row` and `Col` in the column
data and many wells per plate, so that row and column effects can be told
apart from compound effects. The example data have six wells per plate, so
we skip this step:

```{r row-col-effect, eval=FALSE}
sce$Row <- factor(substr(sce$Well, 1, 1))
sce$Col <- factor(as.integer(substr(sce$Well, 2, 3)))
sce <- removeRowColEffect(sce)
```

Note that in the JUMP layout the positive controls sit in the outer
columns of every plate and DMSO in the next columns, so compound and plate
position are confounded, and the same positional effect repeats on every
plate. A comparison between them measures compound and position together.
In your own experiments, randomize the positions of the conditions within
each replicate.

# Exploratory analysis

Single cells are noisy, so average the transformed features per well
(pseudo-bulk) with `scrapper` and look at the wells with a principal
component analysis from `scater`.

```{r aggregate}
aggr <- scrapper::aggregateAcrossCells(
    assay(sce, "tfmfeatures"),
    factors = colData(sce)[, c("Plate", "Well", "Compound")]
)
sce_wells <- SingleCellExperiment(
    assays = list(means = t(t(aggr$sums) / aggr$counts)),
    colData = DataFrame(aggr$combinations, ncells = aggr$counts)
)
sce_wells <- runPCA(sce_wells,
    exprs_values = "means", ncomponents = 10, scale = TRUE
)
plotReducedDim(sce_wells, dimred = "PCA", colour_by = "Compound")
plotReducedDim(sce_wells, dimred = "PCA", colour_by = "Plate")
```

We scale the well means before the PCA (`scale = TRUE`). Robust z-scores
divide by the median absolute deviation, which is close to zero for some
features, such as the minimum intensity at the cell edge, so a few cells get
extreme values that would otherwise dominate the first principal component.
The random forests below are not affected, because trees do not depend on
the scale of a feature.

If the wells separate by compound, the compounds change the cells; if they
separate by plate, there are batch effects between plates. `plotPCACor()`
shows the features most correlated with a principal component, here the
first one.

```{r plot-pca}
plotPCACor(sce_wells, filter_by = 1, top = 15, assay_type = "means")
```

For larger experiments, a nonlinear embedding such as UMAP can show groups
of wells or cells that the first principal components miss, for example
with `scater::runUMAP(sce_wells, exprs_values = "means")` followed by
`scater::plotUMAP(sce_wells, colour_by = "Compound")`.

# Testing a perturbation

## Pre-validated scores

`predictLOO()` compares two levels of a condition (`target`) with the
replicates (`group`) as the folds of the leave-one-out cross-validation.
For each plate, it trains a random forest on the cells of the other plates
to tell AMG900 from DMSO, and scores the cells of the held-out plate with
the probability of AMG900. It does this for all features together and for
each feature group: measurement types, given by the prefix of the feature
names, and channels, given by any part of them.

```{r predict-amg900}
types <- c(
    "AreaShape", "Intensity", "Texture", "RadialDistribution",
    "Granularity", "Correlation"
)
channels <- c("DNA", "RNA", "AGP", "Mito")
set.seed(23)
sce_amg900 <- predictLOO(
    sce,
    target = "Compound", group = "Plate",
    interest_level = "AMG900", reference_level = "DMSO",
    types = types, channels = channels,
    n_threads = 1, progress = FALSE
)
reducedDim(sce_amg900, "prevalidated")[1:3, 1:4]
```

`plotLOO()` shows the scores averaged per plate and compound, one panel per
feature group. If the compound changes the cells, the AMG900 cells of every
plate score higher than the DMSO cells of the same plate.

```{r plot-loo}
plotLOO(sce_amg900, target = "Compound", group = "Plate")
```

## Patient-level tests

`calculateStats()` averages the scores per replicate and condition, takes
the difference $d_p$ for each replicate $p$, and computes the one-sided
paired t-statistic for higher scores in the perturbed condition. It
reports, for each feature group, the $\log_2$ fold change of the mean scores
and a p-value from one of three calibrations.

The **permutation test** (the default) swaps the conditions of whole
replicates, refits all models for every relabeling, and compares the
observed statistic with those of the relabelings. It is exact. Swapping the
conditions of all replicates at once gives the same statistic, so one
replicate keeps its labels: with $n$ replicates there are $2^{n-1}$
relabelings, and the smallest attainable p-value is $2^{1-n}$, here
$1/8$ with four plates. The test refits all models for every relabeling,
so it takes $2^{n-1}$ times as long as `predictLOO()`.

```{r test-permutation}
set.seed(23)
stats_permutation <- calculateStats(sce_amg900,
    target = "Compound", group = "Plate"
)
stats_permutation
```

`r sum(stats_permutation$pvalue == 1/8)` of the
`r nrow(stats_permutation)` feature groups reach the smallest attainable
p-value, 1/8: the observed labels give the largest statistic of all
relabelings. With four replicates, no permutation p-value can be smaller,
however strong the effect, and none can pass a Bonferroni threshold over
several feature groups.

The **corrected t-test** needs no refits. Every replicate is in the training
set of every other replicate's model, so the score differences of different
replicates are positively correlated, and the ordinary t-statistic is too
large. If each score difference is a sum of pairwise interactions with the
other replicates, it is too large by the factor $\sqrt{2(n-1)/(n-2)}$, about
1.73 with four replicates; the corrected t-test divides by it. Its p-values
are not limited to multiples of $2^{1-n}$, but it is approximate.

```{r test-corrected}
stats_corrected <- calculateStats(sce_amg900,
    target = "Compound", group = "Plate", method = "corrected"
)
stats_corrected
```

```{r corrected-range, include=FALSE}
p_range <- format(signif(range(stats_corrected$pvalue), 2), scientific = FALSE)
```

The corrected p-values range from `r p_range[1]` to `r p_range[2]`, below
the floor of the permutation test.

The **Nadeau-Bengio correction** divides by the smaller factor
$\sqrt{(2n-1)/(n-1)}$ of the corrected resampled t-test of Nadeau and
Bengio (2003). It has more power when part of each score difference is
independent of the other replicates, for example noise from the random
seeds of the forests, but with four to six replicates it can exceed the
nominal level when the score differences consist mostly of interactions.

```{r test-nadeau-bengio}
stats_nadeau_bengio <- calculateStats(sce_amg900,
    target = "Compound", group = "Plate", method = "nadeau_bengio"
)
stats_nadeau_bengio
```

`method = "t"` takes p-values from the t-distribution without correction.
It is fast but too liberal, and is meant for ranking many comparisons, not
for inference.

## Summaries

The volcano plot shows one point per feature group, with the $\log_2$ fold
change against the p-value. By default, groups beyond a Bonferroni threshold
of $0.01/G$ for $G$ feature groups and a $\log_2$ fold change of 1 are
labeled. With four replicates, the permutation test cannot reach this
threshold, so we use the corrected t-test and a threshold of 0.05.

```{r plot-volcano}
volcanoPlot(sce_amg900,
    target = "Compound", group = "Plate",
    stats = stats_corrected, p_cutoff = 0.05
)
```

ROC curves and areas under the curve (AUC) describe how well the scores of
each feature group separate the two conditions. Both use the mean score of
each replicate and condition, here eight points per feature group (four
plates times two compounds), so an AUC of 1 means that every AMG900 mean
score lies above every DMSO mean score, whichever plate they come from. The
AUC is a descriptive summary; the tests of `calculateStats()` instead
compare the conditions within each replicate.

```{r plot-roc}
plotAUC(sce_amg900, target = "Compound", group = "Plate")
plotROC(sce_amg900, target = "Compound", group = "Plate")
```

## A weak effect

Dexamethasone changes U2OS cells much less than AMG900. With few
replicates and cells, its scores barely separate from DMSO.

```{r predict-dexamethasone}
set.seed(23)
sce_dex <- predictLOO(
    sce,
    target = "Compound", group = "Plate",
    interest_level = "dexamethasone", reference_level = "DMSO",
    types = types, channels = channels,
    n_threads = 1, progress = FALSE
)
stats_dex <- calculateStats(sce_dex,
    target = "Compound", group = "Plate", method = "corrected"
)
stats_dex
```

The smallest p-value, `r signif(min(stats_dex$pvalue), 2)`, does not pass a
Bonferroni threshold of $0.05/`r nrow(stats_dex)`$ over the feature groups.
Detecting weak effects needs more replicates; the cells per replicate help
only as far as they sharpen each replicate's score difference.

## Run time and parallel computing

`predictLOO()` fits one forest per replicate and feature group, and
`n_threads` sets the number of threads of each fit. The permutation test
refits these forests for every relabeling. The relabelings can run in
parallel with the future framework: set a plan before calling
`calculateStats()`. Keep the product of the number of workers and
`n_threads` at or below the number of cores.

```{r parallel, eval=FALSE}
future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 4)
stats <- calculateStats(sce_amg900, target = "Compound", group = "Plate")
future::plan(future::sequential)
```

# A drug screen with simulated data

`generateData()` simulates a small CellProfiler table with 1,000 cells from
six patients and eight drugs, with 10 shape, 10 intensity, and 10 texture
features named as in real CellProfiler output. Drugs D7 and D8 shift the
texture features; D1 is the control. Every drug is compared with the
control, and the p-values of all comparisons and feature groups are
adjusted together.

```{r simulate}
set.seed(23)
sce_sim <- loadData(generateData())
sce_sim <- transformScale(sce_sim, robust = TRUE)
sce_sim$Drug <- relevel(as.factor(sce_sim$Drug), ref = "D1")
types_sim <- c("AreaShape", "Intensity", "Texture")

sce_list <- map(setdiff(levels(sce_sim$Drug), "D1"), function(drug) {
    predictLOO(
        sce_sim,
        target = "Drug", group = "Patient",
        interest_level = drug, reference_level = "D1",
        types = types_sim, n_threads = 1, progress = FALSE
    )
})
```

For a quick screen of many drugs, the corrected t-test needs no refits. Its
p-values are adjusted with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure over all drugs
and feature groups.

```{r plot-volcano-custom}
p_adj_cutoff <- 0.05
fc_cutoff <- 0.5
tb_stats <- lapply(sce_list, calculateStats,
    target = "Drug", group = "Patient", method = "corrected"
) |>
    bind_rows() |>
    mutate(pvalue_adj = p.adjust(pvalue, method = "BH")) |>
    mutate(Selection = ifelse(
        pvalue_adj < p_adj_cutoff & log2FoldChange > fc_cutoff,
        Target, ""
    ))

tb_stats |>
    ggplot(aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(pvalue_adj), label = Selection)) +
    geom_vline(
        xintercept = c(0, fc_cutoff), alpha = 0.5, linetype = "dashed"
    ) +
    geom_hline(
        yintercept = c(0, -log10(p_adj_cutoff)), alpha = 0.5,
        linetype = "dashed"
    ) +
    geom_point(aes(color = Target)) +
    geom_text_repel(aes(color = Target), max.overlaps = Inf) +
    xlab("log2 fold change") +
    ylab("-log10 p-value (BH adjusted)") +
    facet_wrap(~Feature) +
    ggtitle(paste0("False discovery rate: ", 100 * p_adj_cutoff, "%"))
```
